Letting an AI agent work while you walk away sounds reckless.

The concern is warranted. There are plenty of stories of AI building fragile software with glaring security holes . Agents have also made reckless decisions on their own, like dropping a production database .

It’s sensible to be wary, but don’t dismiss the idea. With the right guardrails and practices in place, you can safely hand work to agents and step away while they do it, shipping high-quality software at a much faster pace. Even in security-sensitive environments, the same approach applies, although you need to be deliberate about where the agent runs and what code leaves your network.

The catch is that the effort doesn’t disappear with asynchronous agents. It shifts to planning before the agent starts and reviewing what it produces. In this article, I’ll cover what it takes to work with asynchronous agents safely and get quality output from them. I won’t compare particular tools or models, since these advance quickly. Instead, I’ll focus on concepts and practices that apply regardless of harness (the tool that runs the agent) and model. Any tools I do mention are just examples I’ve used myself.

## What Is Asynchronous Agentic Development?

Most developers started out using AI for coding in a chat window, either in the browser or as a side panel in their IDE. When these chat tools first arrived, they were mind-blowing. AI agents, though, are so much more than a simple chat interface. An agent can read context, make decisions, and take actions on your behalf, like writing code or debugging an application.

How you work with an agent can be synchronous or asynchronous. In a synchronous setup, you watch the agent work in real time, answering its questions and steering it as it goes. In an asynchronous setup, you hand it a task and walk away. You come back to a pull request that’s ready for review.

Removing that hands-on control lets you scale your effort by running multiple agents in parallel, so you can get through far more work in the same amount of time.

Working asynchronously changes what the quality of the resulting code depends on. When you work synchronously, you’re the safety net. You notice the agent drifting, correct it mid-task, and catch mistakes as they happen. When you work asynchronously, nothing catches a mistake until the work is done, so the result depends on what you set up beforehand: how clear your specs are, how safe your environments are, and how good your checks are.

Read the diagram from left to right. You plan the work and its context. The agent implements it in a sandbox, running tests as it goes. If the same wrong assumption keeps appearing, you update the steering files so it’s corrected for every future task.

The workflow doesn’t remove the human from the loop. It moves your attention to the two points that matter most: the plan before the agent starts and the pull request when it finishes, rather than every step in between.

That means letting go of some control, which isn’t easy when you have strong preferences about how code is formatted and structured. As someone who’s opinionated about code style, I found this challenging at first. But you aren’t lowering your standards, you’re moving them out of your head and into explicit guardrails. For the standards you care about, you set up linters and formatters in CI and let the pipeline enforce them. For the rest, like whether a brace goes on a new line, you accept that it no longer matters.

### When Not to Work Asynchronously

Asynchronous work suits tasks you can fully specify up front. It’s a poor fit when you can’t write the acceptance criteria yet. Exploratory work, such as prototyping with an unfamiliar library, investigating a hard-to-reproduce bug or settling a design question, depends on your feedback, and an agent working alone will fill the gaps with guesses. Do that work synchronously, and turn what you learn into decisions and tasks that you can delegate.

## Less Risky Than It Looks

An asynchronous agent is only as risky as the access you give it.

If your environment isn’t set up correctly, nothing stops an agent from reading sensitive files like your SSH private key and sending it to a remote server with a cURL request. Or, an agent might send a PR with broken code and merge it in automatically without any human review or automated checks. If you don’t have pipelines or automated checks, you’ll miss potential secrets being committed or malicious packages being installed.

Approving every action by hand isn’t the fix either. Your attention fades the longer a session runs, and by the fiftieth approval you’re barely reading what you’re approving . Rules don’t fade, so the safer approach is to enforce them automatically and let the agent work within them.

Most of those controls are ones a security team already expects for human developers: branch protection and required reviews stop broken code from merging on its own, and pipeline checks catch committed secrets and malicious packages. That’s what makes this approach workable in security-sensitive environments. Agents add a couple of new risks. One is that they can be steered by text they read, so the sandbox has to assume a hijacked agent and leave it with no production credentials and a restricted network. Another is that they can optimise for a green pipeline rather than correct behaviour, so the tests need protecting too.

The rest of this article walks through a workflow that builds those rules in at every stage, from planning the work to reviewing the pull request.

## Plan Before You Delegate

Working with asynchronous agents shouldn’t involve delegating all architectural decisions to the agent itself. You’re still responsible for the final output, and the only way of ensuring it aligns with your long-term vision for the project is to plan thoroughly before delegating work.

### Make the Technical Decisions Yourself

Your role as a software developer shifts from writing code to knowing how to architect and design the codebase. The agent can write code syntax, but it’s important that you still make the technical decisions yourself.

Why? Because every technical decision comes with tradeoffs. There’s no silver bullet. You’re far more aware of the long-term vision for the project and are the best person to decide which technical decisions align with that vision.

Some of these decisions include picking the right technology stack that best supports your future goals. If you have licensing requirements, you need to pick the dependencies that align with those requirements. If your software has a public API, you should be the one deciding what the endpoint contracts should look like. Of course you can (and should) use AI to help you research these decisions, but you are the one who makes the final call.

Once you’ve made a decision, write it down along with the reasoning behind it, even if it’s just a few lines in an architectural decision record (ADR) in your repository. That way, the agent implements the decision instead of second-guessing it, and your tasks can point back to it. From my experience, it also stops future agents from going back to a previous option that we deliberately steered away from.

Any open question you don’t answer will be answered by the agent. And with the agent’s limited context and knowledge, that decision is usually the wrong one.

### Break Down the Work Logically

Once the decisions are made, have the agent propose a breakdown of the work to be done and then refine it yourself. Review the list before any code gets written. A bad split is far more expensive after the agent has already started working on the codebase.

When breaking down the work, slice it vertically, not horizontally. A horizontal split gives you tasks like “add the Payment entity”, “add the payment service”, and “add the payments controller”. None of those can be tested on their own, and no reviewer can tell whether they’re right until all three land. A vertical slice delivers something testable end to end. For the payments feature, that might look like this:

- Record a full payment against an invoice (domain rule, handler, endpoint, and tests).

- Support partial payments and track the outstanding balance (after 1).

- Reject payments on voided invoices (after 1).

- Add an endpoint that lists an invoice’s payments (after 1).

Each task above is a complete unit of work that can be tested independently of the others. Slices 2, 3 and 4 only depend on the first one, so once it lands, three agents can work on them in parallel. They will likely touch some of the same files, like the Invoice entity, so list the files each task is expected to change and sequence any that overlap. The tasks should be sized so that an agent can easily implement them in a session with optional subagents to delegate work to. It should also result in PRs that are small enough to be reviewed by a human in a timely manner.

When I first started working with multiple agents asynchronously, I ran into a number of merge conflicts. They would take two to three times longer to resolve than the actual task implementation took. It made me realise the importance of upfront technical planning of tasks. Having a clear, well-defined task with clear blockers and dependencies, along with a list of existing files that the task will most likely touch, helped me avoid ugly merge conflicts down the line.

### Write Well-Defined Tasks

Each slice from the breakdown becomes a task. A well-sliced task isn’t automatically a well-defined one. A task is well-defined when an agent can finish it without needing additional answers from you halfway through the process that would change the architecture or outcome.

Most of us would write the task for a colleague like this:

Title: Add payments to invoices Customers should be able to pay invoices. Add a REST endpoint to support this.

This was never a good ticket for a human either. Your colleague just absorbs the cost, either by asking you follow-up questions or by drawing on experience from similar features they’ve built and their knowledge of your domain and standards. An agent has neither. It will fill the gaps with its own assumptions, and some of those will be wrong simply because it lacks the background.

An agent needs more than a single vague sentence. The task description should give it the relevant context, set a clear scope so it neither over- nor under-engineers the solution, and state the acceptance criteria that define “done”. The ticket above should look more like this:

Title: Record a full payment against an invoice ## Context Part of the "Invoice payments" feature. It should follow the decision made in ADR-0007 where payment initiation is a sub-resource of an invoice on the REST API. Amounts are always decimal numbers with up to two decimal places. ## Scope - Add ` POST /invoices/{invoiceId}/payments ` for a single payment that settles the invoice in full. - Add a Payment entity (Domain), a ` RecordPayment ` command and handler (Application), and the endpoint (API). ## Acceptance Criteria - Returns a 201 Created with the created payment identifier. - The invoice moves from "Sent" to "Paid" when the payment succeeds. The payment amount must equal the outstanding invoice balance. - Returns a 404 Not Found if the invoice does not exist. - Returns a 422 Unprocessable Entity if the invoice is a draft, is already paid, or the payment amount does not equal the outstanding invoice balance. - Domain rules are covered by unit tests, and the endpoint by integration tests against a test database. ## Out of Scope - Partial payments, refunds, payment history and payment notifications.
